questions.q: What does an HTTP 429 status code mean when calling an API?
options: You've been rate-limited — you've exceeded the allowed number of requests in a given time window
The requested resource doesn't exist
The server crashed unexpectedly
The request succeeded but returned no data
questions.explain: 429 Too Many Requests is the standard status code APIs return when a client has exceeded its allowed request rate. It's a normal, well-formed HTTP response, not a crash.

questions.q: What does a `Retry-After` response header tell a client?
options: The exact error message to display to the user
How many total requests remain in the current time window
The API's current server load percentage
How long (typically in seconds) to wait before retrying the request
questions.explain: When present, Retry-After gives a concrete wait time, letting a client retry exactly when the server expects capacity to be available again, rather than guessing.

questions.q: In an exponential backoff retry loop, what happens to the wait time after each failed attempt?
options: It stays exactly the same every time
It resets to zero after each attempt
It roughly doubles each time (e.g. 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s), rather than retrying at a fixed interval
It decreases after each attempt
questions.explain: Exponential backoff doubles (or otherwise increases) the wait time after each consecutive failure, so early retries happen quickly while repeated failures space retries out further, reducing pressure on an already-struggling service.

questions.q: Why does a well-behaved API client implement backoff and retries instead of immediately retrying a 429 response as fast as possible?
options: Retrying immediately is actually the recommended approach
Rate limits exist to keep a shared service usable for everyone; hammering the API immediately after a 429 just triggers more 429s and adds load
Python doesn't allow back-to-back requests
429 responses can only be retried once per day
questions.explain: Rate limits protect a shared service's capacity. Retrying immediately after a 429 is counterproductive — it's likely to hit the same limit again and adds unnecessary load, which is why backing off (via Retry-After or exponential backoff) is the standard, cooperative approach.

questions.q: In the exponential backoff loop `wait = 1; ...; time.sleep(wait); wait *= 2`, what is the wait time before the 3rd retry attempt?
options: 1 second
2 seconds
4 seconds
8 seconds
questions.explain: Starting at wait=1, each failed attempt doubles it: 1s before the first retry, 2s before the second, 4s before the third — doubling every time a 429 is hit again.
